Latent Anomaly Knowledge Excavation: Unveiling Sparse Sensitive Neurons in Vision-Language Models

Excavate anomaly-sensitive neurons already present in a vision-language model using a small set of normal samples.

Li Shaotian

April 9, 2026 ·ACM Multimedia 2026CCF-A ·3-minute read ·Read the paper ·PDF
1Why this matters 2How it works 3What the study finds 4What this means

The short version

LAKE uses a small collection of normal images to locate anomaly-sensitive units in a frozen vision-language model. Patch-level structural deviations and cross-modal semantic signals are combined into an anomaly score. The backbone supplies the representation; normal examples help identify how that representation should be read.

The approach links localization to detection without gradient-based backbone adaptation. Quantitative evaluations and spatial anomaly maps examine whether the selected signals can identify unfamiliar defects and localize their regions.

SparseSensitive-neuron representation
NormalSamples used for localization
0Gradient-based backbone updates

Normal examples can reveal which parts of a pretrained representation are useful for detecting the abnormal.

Why this matters

Treating a VLM as a black-box feature extractor can obscure which internal signals support anomaly detection. LAKE examines whether those signals can be selected and elicited directly.

How it works

  1. Use a minimal set of normal samples to identify anomaly-sensitive neurons in the pretrained model.
  2. Isolate the selected signals to construct a compact representation of normality.
  3. Combine visual structural deviations with cross-modal semantic activations for anomaly scoring.

What the study finds

Evaluation on industrial anomaly-detection benchmarks reports strong performance together with neuron-level interpretability. The approach uses normal samples and does not train a new backbone.

What this means

For anomaly detection, limited defect data is a structural condition of the problem. A useful system must extract diagnostic value from what normality makes observable. LAKE frames that task as selecting and reading pretrained knowledge at the appropriate internal locations.

This gives an interpretable way to study adaptation under scarce evidence: which units normal samples select, what deviations they detect, and how performance changes with the normal support set. The same questions help identify when pretrained knowledge is insufficient for a new inspection environment.
